questions.question: what's actually in a burrito bowl

relevant.why: The bowl rows are where the published composition of a bowl is; any one of them answers what a bowl is made of.

questions.why: The plainest knowledge question there is, and the golden set's first knowledge case. It is here as the floor: a retriever that misses this misses everything below it.

questions.question: what comes on a steak burrito

relevant.why: The Steak Burrito's own row.

questions.why: Two proper nouns in five words, which is the shape RFC-001 section 08 built the keyword half for. If the ablation's arms differ anywhere, they differ here.

questions.question: what kinds of rice do you have

relevant.why: The rice rows are the published choices.

questions.why: A category question rather than an item question: the answer is a family, and any member of it is a correct first hit.

questions.question: what beans do you serve

relevant.why: The bean rows are the published choices.

questions.why: The same shape as the rice question, on a family the vision lane also has a slot for -- so a retrieval regression here shows up twice.

questions.question: do you have guacamole

relevant.why: Guacamole's own row.

questions.why: A one-word question whose whole content is a proper noun. The vector half has an opinion about the Spanish word; only the lexical half has one about this menu.

questions.question: what is barbacoa

relevant.why: The barbacoa rows: the fillings whose published primary_filling is it.

questions.why: RFC-001 section 08 names barbacoa by name as the token embeddings place badly. It is in the set so that claim has a number attached to it, and it is expected to go unscored against any corpus slice that does not carry the item -- which is the resolution check working, not a miss.

questions.question: are the black beans cooked in the same pot as the chicken
questions.why: Preparation is not something Chipotle publishes. The corpus holds the beans row and the chicken row, so the retriever will find plausible neighbours -- which is exactly the near-miss the confidence rule is supposed to catch rather than rank.

questions.question: is the chicken halal
questions.why: A published-certification question the published pages do not answer. The chicken row is a very good lexical match and a very bad answer.

questions.question: what's vegetarian here
questions.why: The diet tag `vege` is published on Chipotle's chart and is not a column of the chunk schema, so chip_chat.search.query puts it in `unapplied` rather than approximating it. This question is in the negative set to hold that refusal to a number: a confident answer here would be a dietary claim about food that nobody published.

questions.question: how many calories are in a chicken bowl

relevant.why: The Chicken Bowl row carries the published figure.

questions.why: The golden set's nutrition case. Calories are a filterable column of the chunk schema, so this is also the question whose answer a constrained query would have to narrow on.

questions.question: how many calories in a steak burrito

relevant.why: The Steak Burrito row carries the published figure.

questions.why: The second half of the comparative below, asked on its own, so that a failure on the comparison can be told apart from a failure on either item.

questions.question: which has fewer calories, the chicken bowl or the steak burrito

relevant.why: One side of the comparison.
The other side.

questions.why: #49 calls out the comparative case, and it is the clearest question in the set for why recall is counted over labels: an answer that found one of the two items is half right, and a hit-or-miss score would call it right.

questions.question: how many calories are in the chips

relevant.why: The Chips row.

questions.why: A side rather than an entree. The menu's non-entree rows are shorter and carry fewer searchable words, which is where a lexical half has least to work with.

questions.question: how many calories does guac add

relevant.why: Guacamole's row carries the published figure.

questions.why: `guac` is what a visitor types and `Guacamole` is what the menu publishes. The one question in the nutrition category where the lexical half is at a disadvantage and the vector half should earn its place.

questions.question: how many calories were in a chicken bowl last year
questions.why: The corpus is one harvest. It has no history, so a question about a past figure has no answer in it however good the retrieval is -- and the chicken bowl row is a near-perfect lexical match for it.

questions.question: does the cheese have dairy in it

relevant.why: Cheese's row carries the published dairy mark.

questions.why: The golden set's allergen case, and the one every allergen number in this report is anchored to. Note that the question mentions the allergen without negating it -- chip_chat.search.query refuses to build a filter from a mention, and this is the question that would break if it ever stopped refusing.

questions.question: is the guacamole dairy free

relevant.why: Guacamole's row carries its published marks.

questions.why: The negated phrasing of the question above, on an item whose answer is the other one. A retriever that returns the cheese row here has answered a different question confidently.

questions.question: are the chips ok if i'm allergic to dairy

relevant.why: The Chips row carries its published marks.

questions.why: Phrased as a person actually asks it, with the allergy in the second clause. The published marks are the only thing that can answer it and they are on one row.

questions.question: does the white rice have anything in it i should know about

relevant.why: The White Rice row carries its published marks.

questions.why: An allergen question that never says the word. If the lexical half is carrying the allergen category on the word `allergy`, this is the question that shows it.

questions.question: will the steak be safe for my severe soy allergy

relevant.why: The Steak Burrito row carries the published marks for the steak the question is about.

questions.why: The golden set scores this on the agent's refusal to make a safety judgement. Here it is scored on the half that has to work first: the published marks have to be in front of the model before it can decline to go beyond them.

questions.question: what can i get without any dairy
questions.why: Scored on the filter rather than on the ranking, because a filter is what #49 answers it with. It carries no relevant place on purpose: the correct answer set is every published item whose marks exclude dairy, and labelling three of them would be picking favourites among interchangeable rows.

questions.question: can i get a bowl with no dairy

relevant.why: The bowl rows: the question is about bowls, and the filter decides which of them may be offered.

questions.why: The one question in the set scored on both mechanisms at once. A retriever can rank the bowls perfectly and still hand back one it should have filtered out, and only a question with both labels can show that.

questions.question: how do i know if something is safe with my allergy

relevant.why: Chipotle's own caveat about what its marks do and do not promise. The published sentence, not a paraphrase of it.

questions.why: The published caveat is a chunk kind of its own in the schema, so this question is how the set finds out whether the corpus under test actually carries one. Against a corpus that does not, it goes unscored and says so, which is more useful than a miss nobody can act on.

questions.question: is the kitchen free of gluten cross contact
questions.why: A preparation question wearing an allergen question's clothes. The safety-critical negative: every word in it matches the corpus and none of the corpus answers it, so a retriever that reports this as grounded has produced the most dangerous kind of near-miss this project has.

questions.question: which items are safe for a peanut allergy
questions.why: Chipotle publishes four allergen marks and peanut is not one of them, so there is no published answer -- and an unmarked item is not a promise. docs/decisions/allergen-absence.md is the argument; this is the number.

questions.question: how do points work

relevant.heading: Okay, so how does Chipotle Rewards work?
relevant.why: The FAQ entry that answers it in one paragraph.
The rewards page's own explanation of the earn rate.

questions.why: The golden set's rewards case. Two published places answer it and they are in two different documents, which is what makes it worth more than a hit-or-miss score.

questions.question: do my points expire

relevant.heading: Do points expire?
relevant.why: The FAQ entry, in the visitor's words.
The terms' own section, which is where the 365 days is binding.
relevant.heading: TRACKING YOUR ACCOUNT; POINTS EXPIRATION

relevant.why: The rewards page's shorter answer to the same question.

questions.why: Three published places, in three documents, saying the same thing at three levels of formality. The question in the set with the most to recall, and the one where a top-3 that spends all three slots in one document is visible.

questions.question: what can i redeem my points for

relevant.heading: What can I redeem my points for?
relevant.why: The FAQ entry.
The rewards exchange section.

questions.why: Nearly the FAQ heading verbatim, which is the easiest thing a lexical half can be asked to do. It is in the set as the ceiling: if the keyword arm misses this, the index is wrong rather than the ranking.

questions.question: who is allowed to join chipotle rewards

relevant.why: The terms' eligibility section.
relevant.heading: ELIGIBILITY

questions.why: A one-word heading in a long legal document. The heading is searchable and weighted, so this is the question that says whether that weighting is doing anything.

questions.question: which purchases earn points

relevant.why: The terms' section on accumulating points.
relevant.heading: ACCUMULATING POINTS

questions.why: The visitor's words and the document's words share no content word. Where the vector half is supposed to earn its place inside a policy document rather than on a menu row.

questions.question: do catering orders earn rewards points

relevant.heading: How do I get Chipotle Rewards points for my catering orders?
relevant.why: The FAQ entry about exactly this.

questions.why: Sits between the rewards and ordering categories, which is why it is worth having: a retriever that has learned `catering` means the ordering FAQ will get this one wrong in a way no single-category question shows.

questions.question: if i have a dispute do i have to go to arbitration

relevant.why: The terms' arbitration agreement.
relevant.heading: ARBITRATION AGREEMENT

questions.why: The longest and least food-like passage in the corpus. It is here so the set is not made entirely of short rows, which is the shape a chunking regression shows up in first.

questions.question: can i cancel an order after i've placed it

relevant.heading: Can I cancel my online or mobile order after I've submitted it?
relevant.why: The FAQ entry for an online or mobile order.

relevant.heading: Can I cancel my delivery after I've submitted my order?
relevant.why: The FAQ entry for a delivery order, which is the same question asked about the other channel and is genuinely an answer to a visitor who did not say which they placed.

questions.why: The golden set's cancellation case. The visitor did not say which kind of order, and two published entries answer it -- so a correct retrieval surfaces both rather than picking one and sounding certain.

questions.question: can i cancel a delivery once it's on its way

relevant.heading: Can I cancel my delivery after I've submitted my order?
relevant.why: The FAQ entry for a delivery order.

questions.why: The same question with the channel named. The pair with the one above is how the set tells `found the right document` apart from `found the right half of it`.

questions.question: how do i get a refund on a delivery order

relevant.heading: Who do I contact regarding delivery payment issues, including refund requests?
relevant.why: The FAQ entry that covers refund requests on delivery orders.

questions.why: The golden set's refund case, narrowed to the channel the published pages actually answer for. Asking it unqualified would be labelling a question whose answer is not in the corpus as though it were.

questions.question: do you do catering

relevant.heading: Does Chipotle cater?
relevant.why: The FAQ entry.

questions.why: Four words, all of them common. Nothing here is a proper noun, so it is the ordering category's version of the question the vector half should be best at.

questions.question: who do i talk to about a catering order i already placed

relevant.heading: Who do I reach out to for questions regarding my catering order?
relevant.why: The FAQ entry for questions about a placed catering order.

questions.why: Its near-neighbour is the question above, and both contain `catering`. A pair that shares its rarest word is how a set measures ranking rather than matching.

questions.question: can i get cash back for the balance on my gift card

relevant.heading: How do I get cash back for my Chipotle gift card balance?
relevant.why: The FAQ entry.

questions.why: A corner of the corpus nothing else in the set touches, which is what keeps the ordering category from being four questions about cancelling.

questions.question: what time does the store on market street close today
questions.why: Store hours are not in the published corpus this project harvests, and they are the single most likely thing a visitor asks that it cannot answer. A confident answer here is an invented fact about a real place.

questions.question: how much do you pay the people who work here
questions.why: Far outside the corpus in subject matter, so it is the negative that says whether the confidence rule is doing anything at all or whether the corpus is simply always a bit relevant.
